content.intro: This lesson covers Spreadsheet Architecture and Design as part of Professional Spreadsheet Engineering and Specialized Applications. It follows the attached Excel curriculum, with an emphasis on small examples and verification.
content.why_it_matters: Spreadsheet Architecture and Design contributes to reliable business reporting and professional spreadsheet delivery. Document assumptions, verify results independently, and separate optional platform tools from core Excel behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Spreadsheet Architecture and Design focuses on the following parts of the supplied syllabus: Separating input, processing, and output; Worksheet and workbook structure; Clear calculation dependencies; Designing for maintenance. Keep the underlying source data visible and make each assumption explicit.

content_blocks.code: Raw input → organized worksheet/table → calculation or analysis → validated output
content_blocks.expected_output: A basic worksheet workflow separates raw inputs from calculations and outputs, then checks the result against the source.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a copy of the workbook; keep clear headers, avoid blank rows inside tables, and compare row counts/totals before and after a structural edit.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Work in a duplicate workbook or a scratch sheet. Restore the input range and formula/code to the original state, clear filters or selections, then rerun the same test cases. Record expected and actual behavior rather than assuming a successful result.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with a small, known dataset for spreadsheet architecture and design. Apply the example above, compute or inspect at least one result independently, then deliberately try a blank, duplicate, boundary, or not-found case where relevant.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small worksheet or workbook section that demonstrates spreadsheet architecture and design. Use clear headers, label units and assumptions, and capture expected versus actual output for a normal case and an edge case. Where the concept requires a specialized Excel feature, first verify that feature is available in your Excel edition.

content.task: Build or inspect an Excel example that demonstrates spreadsheet architecture and design; use the example to verify one normal and one edge case, and write down any version or tool dependency.
task_acceptance_criteria: The worksheet/workflow uses a clear, labeled source range and explicit assumptions.
The learner records an expected output and independently compares it with the actual result.
At least one relevant edge case is checked; data and formula errors are not silently concealed.
The workbook is saved as a copy and compatibility/security/accessibility notes are followed where relevant.
hints: Reduce the problem to a small range with known values before scaling it up.
Inspect cell values and formulas, not only displayed formatting; verify data types, references and range boundaries.
Compare expected versus actual results and check the Microsoft documentation for version-specific functions or tools.
content.expected_output: A basic worksheet workflow separates raw inputs from calculations and outputs, then checks the result against the source.
common_mistakes: Assuming the displayed format is the same as the stored value or data type.
Using an incorrect range boundary, a mismatched lookup key, or an unverified assumption.
Trusting a result without comparing it with a known calculation or checking a failure/edge case.
summary: Spreadsheet Architecture and Design supports the workflow in Professional Spreadsheet Engineering and Specialized Applications.
Use a small example, make assumptions visible, and verify the result against the source.
Check target-version availability and keep a clean copy before making high-impact changes.
